intro: The third group turns from sense-desire itself to five specific mental states that cover over ("hinder") a mind trying to enter concentration — a taxonomy that becomes foundational across the whole later tradition of Buddhist meditation instruction.

zh:
第三、棄五蓋者：一者、貪欲蓋；二、瞋恚蓋；三、睡眠蓋；四、掉悔蓋；五、疑蓋。第一、棄貪欲者，前說外五塵中生欲，今約內意根生欲。所謂行者端坐修禪，心生欲覺，念念相續，覆蓋善心，令不生長，覺已應棄。所以者何？如術婆伽欲心內發，尚能燒身，況復心生欲火而不燒諸善法？復次，貪欲之人，去道甚遠。所以者何？欲為種種惱亂住處，若心著欲，無由近道，如除蓋偈說：
入道慚愧人，持鉢福眾生。
云何縱塵欲，沈沒於五情？
已捨於五欲，棄之而不顧，
如何還欲得，如愚自食吐？
諸欲求時苦，得時多怖畏，
失時懷悲惱，一切無樂處。
諸欲患如是，已訶能捨之，
得福禪定樂，則不為所欺。
如是等種種因緣訶貪欲蓋，如《摩訶衍》中訶欲偈說。
en: Third, abandoning the five hindrances: first, the hindrance of desire; second, the hindrance of anger; third, the hindrance of sleep; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and regret; fifth, the hindrance of doubt.

First, abandoning the hindrance of desire: what was described earlier concerns desire arising from the five external objects; here, desire arising from the internal faculty of intention is addressed. This refers to a practitioner sitting upright in the cultivation of dhyāna, giving rise to a mind of desire that continues moment after moment, covering over the wholesome mind and preventing it from growing — once this is recognized, it should be abandoned. Why is this? Even Shupojia, when the mind of desire blazed up within him, was able to burn his own body — how much more should the fire of desire arising in the mind be feared, for it burns away every wholesome dharma? Furthermore, a person given over to desire is very far from the path. Why is this? Desire is the very dwelling-place of every kind of vexation and disturbance; if the mind clings to desire, there is no way to draw near the path — as the verse on removing this hindrance says:
"One who has entered the path with a sense of shame, holding the bowl to bring merit to sentient beings —
How could such a person indulge in worldly desire, sinking into the five faculties of feeling?
Having already renounced the five desires, cast aside and given no further thought —
How could one wish to have them back again, like a fool who eats their own vomit?
Every desire brings suffering while it is sought, and, once obtained, brings much fear;
And when it is lost, sorrow and vexation follow — nowhere in it is there any true joy.
Since the affliction of every desire is like this, having rejected it, one is able to let it go,
And, gaining the joy of merit and dhyāna-concentration, one is no longer deceived by it."
Through causes and conditions such as these, the hindrance of desire is rejected, as the verse rejecting desire in the Mahāyāna treatise explains.

zh:
第二、棄瞋恚蓋者，瞋是生諸不善法之根本，墜諸惡道之因緣，法樂之怨家，善心之大賊，種種惡口之府藏。復次，行者於坐時思惟：「此人惱我及惱我親，讚歎我怨。」思惟過去、未來亦如是，是為九惱。惱故生瞋，瞋故生恨，恨故生怨，怨故欲加報惱彼。瞋、恨、怨、惱覺觀覆心，故名為蓋。當急棄之，無令增長。如釋提婆那以偈問佛：
何物殺安隱？何物殺無憂？
何物毒之根，吞滅一切善？
佛以偈答言：
殺瞋則安隱，殺瞋則無憂。
瞋為毒之根，瞋滅一切善。
如是知已，當修慈忍，以除滅之，令心清淨，如《摩訶衍》中佛教弟子訶瞋偈，是中應廣說。
en:
Second, abandoning the hindrance of anger: anger is the very root from which every unwholesome dharma arises, the condition that causes one to fall into the evil destinies, the enemy of the joy of the Dharma, the great thief of the wholesome mind, the storehouse of every kind of evil speech. Furthermore, a practitioner, while sitting, may reflect: "This person has vexed me, and has vexed those dear to me, and has praised those I resent." Reflecting in the same way about the past and the future gives nine grounds for vexation in all. From vexation, anger arises; from anger, resentment arises; from resentment, enmity arises; and from enmity comes the wish to retaliate and vex the other in turn. Anger, resentment, enmity, and vexation, together with coarse and subtle discursive thought about them, cover over the mind — hence this is called a hindrance. It must be swiftly abandoned, and not allowed to grow. As Śakra, Lord of the Devas, once asked the Buddha in verse:
"What thing, once slain, brings peace? What thing, once slain, brings freedom from sorrow?
What is the very root of poison, that swallows up and destroys every wholesome thing?"
The Buddha answered in verse:
"Slay anger, and peace is attained; slay anger, and freedom from sorrow is attained.
Anger is the very root of poison; anger destroys every wholesome thing."
Knowing this, one should cultivate loving-kindness and patience in order to remove and extinguish it, purifying the mind, as the verse in which the Buddha teaches his disciples to reject anger, in the Mahāyāna treatise, explains in full.

The "nine grounds for vexation" (九惱) generalize a single grievance across three tenses (past, present, future) and three targets (harm to me, harm to those I love, praise of those I resent) — a compact but exhaustive map of how one triggering thought multiplies into sustained anger. Notice the chain it produces: vexation → anger → resentment → enmity → the wish to retaliate, each step compounding the last.

zh:
第三、訶睡眠蓋者，內心惛暗，名為睡；放恣支節，委臥垂熟，名為眠。復次，意識惛冥，名為睡；五情闇蔽惛熟，名為眠。以是因緣，名為睡眠蓋。《阿毘曇》中說：「為增心數法，能破今世三事，謂樂、利樂、福德；又能破今世、後世實樂。」如此惡法，最為不善。何以故？餘蓋情覺可除，眠如死人，無所覺識。以不覺故，難可除滅。如有菩薩教睡眠弟子言：
汝起勿抱死屍臥，種種不淨假名人，
如得重病箭入體，諸苦痛集安可眠？
如人被縛將去殺，災害垂至安可眠？
結賊未滅害未除，如共毒蛇同室居，
亦如臨陣白刃間，爾時云何而可眠？
眠為大暗無所見，日日欺誑奪人明。
以眠覆心無所見，如是大失安可眠？
如是等種種訶眠蓋，警覺無常，滅損睡眠，令無惛覆。若睡眠心重，當用禪鎮、禪杖等却之也。
en: Third, rejecting the hindrance of sleep: dullness and darkness within the mind is called drowsiness; the limbs going slack, the body sinking into deep repose, is called slumber. Furthermore, dullness and obscurity in mental consciousness is called drowsiness; darkness and obscuration covering the five faculties of feeling, sunk into deep repose, is called slumber. For these reasons, this is called the hindrance of sleep. As the Abhidharma says: "As a mental factor that grows stronger the more it is indulged, it is able to destroy three things in the present life — happiness, benefit and joy, and merit — and is further able to destroy the true happiness of both this life and lives to come." Such an unwholesome dharma as this is the most unwholesome of all. Why is this? The remaining hindrances can still be recognized and removed by feeling and awareness, but sleep is like a dead person, possessing no awareness or consciousness whatsoever. Because there is no awareness of it, it is hard to remove and extinguish.

There was once a bodhisattva who taught a sleeping disciple, saying:
"Rise — do not lie there embracing a corpse, this provisionally-named person made of every impurity;
As one struck by a grave illness, an arrow lodged in the body, every pain and suffering gathered — how can you sleep?
As one who is bound and being led away to execution, disaster imminent — how can you sleep?
The thief of the fetters not yet slain, the harm not yet removed — it is like dwelling in the same room as a venomous snake,
Or standing amid drawn blades on the very edge of battle — how, at such a time, could you possibly sleep?
Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing can be seen, day after day deceiving and robbing a person of clarity.
With sleep covering the mind, nothing at all can be seen — with such a great loss as this, how can you sleep?"
Through various means such as these, the hindrance of sleep is rejected, awakening one to impermanence and diminishing sleep, so that no dullness remains to cover the mind. If the mind is heavily weighed down by sleep, a meditation-weight or meditation-staff and the like should be used to drive it off.

zh:
第四、棄掉悔者，掉有三種：一、身；二、口；三、心。身掉者，身好遊走諸雜戲謔，坐不暫安。口掉者，好喜吟詠，諍競是非，無益談論及世俗言話等。心掉者，心情放蕩，縱意攀緣，思惟文藝、世間才技、諸惡覺觀等，名為心掉。掉之為法，破出家心，如人攝心猶不得定，何況掉散。掉散之人，如無鉤醉象、穴鼻駱駝，不可禁制，如偈說：
汝已剃頭著染衣，執持瓦鉢行乞食，
云何樂著戲掉法，放逸縱情失法利？
既無法利，又失世樂，覺其過已，當急棄之。悔者若掉，無悔則不成蓋。何以故？掉時未在緣中，故後欲入定時，大悔前所作，憂惱覆心，故名為蓋。復次，悔有二種：一者、因掉後生悔，如前說；二者、如大重罪人，常懷怖畏，悔箭入心，堅不可拔。如偈說：
不應作而作，應作而不作，
煩惱火所燒，後世墮惡道。
若人罪能悔，悔已莫復憂，
如是心安樂，不應常念著。
若有二種悔，若應作不作，
不應作而作，是則愚人相。
不以心悔故，不作而能作，
諸惡事已作，不能令不作。
如是種種因緣訶掉悔蓋，心神清淨，無有覆蓋，常在善心，則寂然安樂。以是因緣，心得法喜。
en:
Fourth, abandoning restlessness and regret. Restlessness is of three kinds: bodily, verbal, and mental. Bodily restlessness is a fondness for wandering about and engaging in every kind of frivolous jesting, unable to sit still even briefly. Verbal restlessness is a fondness for chanting and reciting, contending over right and wrong, and idle conversation and worldly talk of no benefit. Mental restlessness is a mind given over to dissipation, indulging the intention to chase after objects, occupying itself with literary arts, worldly skills and talents, and every kind of unwholesome discursive thought — this is called mental restlessness. Restlessness as a phenomenon breaks down the very mind of one who has gone forth from home; even one who gathers the mind carefully still fails to attain concentration — how much more so one who is restless and scattered? A person who is restless and scattered is like an intoxicated elephant with no hook to guide it, or a camel with a pierced nose that cannot be controlled — as the verse says:
"You have already shaved your head and put on the dyed robe, taking up the clay bowl to walk for alms —
Why, then, delight in attachment to frivolous, restless ways, indulging laxly and losing the benefit of the Dharma?"
Having thus lost both the benefit of the Dharma and worldly happiness alike, once this fault is recognized, it must be swiftly abandoned.

As for regret: where there is restlessness but no regret, it does not form a hindrance. Why is this? At the very moment of restlessness, the mind is not yet fixed on any object — but afterward, when one wishes to enter concentration, great regret arises over what was done before, and worry and vexation cover the mind; hence this is called a hindrance. Furthermore, regret is of two kinds: first, regret arising afterward because of restlessness, as just described; second, regret like that of a person who has committed a grave and serious offense, constantly harboring fear, the arrow of regret lodged firmly in the heart and unable to be pulled out. As the verse says:
"What should not be done, is done; what should be done, is left undone —
Burned by the fire of affliction, one falls, in lives to come, into an evil destiny.
If a person is able to repent of an offense, once repented, let there be no further worry —
With a mind thus at ease and joyful, one should not dwell on it constantly.
But if there are these two kinds of regret — over what should have been done and was not,
Or over what should not have been done and was — this is the mark of the foolish.
It is not that, through regretting in the mind, what was left undone can now be done,
Nor that whatever evil has already been done can be made undone."
Through causes and conditions such as these, the hindrance of restlessness and regret is rejected; the mind and spirit become pure, with no covering hindrance remaining, constantly abiding in a wholesome mind, and thus becoming still and at ease. Through this, the mind attains the joy of the Dharma.

zh:
第五、棄疑蓋者，以疑覆故，於諸法中不得定心。定心無故，於佛法中空無所獲，譬如人入寶山，若無有手，無所能取。復次，通疑甚多，未必障定。今正障定疑者，謂三種疑：一者、疑自；二者、疑師；三者、疑法。疑自者，若人作是念：「我諸根暗鈍，罪垢深重，非其器乎！」作此自疑，定法終不發也。欲去之者，無得自輕，以宿世善根難測故。二、疑師者：「彼人威儀相貌如是，自尚無道，何能教我？」作是疑慢，即為障定。欲除之法，如《摩訶衍》中說：「如臭皮囊中金，以貪金故，不可棄臭皮囊。行者亦爾，師雖不清淨，亦應生佛想。」此事如《摩訶衍》中釋薩陀波淪求善知識具明，是中應廣說。三、疑法者，世人多執本心，於所受之法不能即信，故不敬心受行。若心生猶豫，即法不染神。何以故？如訶疑偈中說：
如人在岐道，疑惑無所取，
諸法實相中，疑亦復如是。
疑故不勤求，諸法之實相，
是疑從癡生，惡中之惡者。
善不善法中，生死及涅槃，
定實真有法，於中莫生疑。
汝若懷疑惑，死生獄吏縛，
如師子搏鹿，不能得解脫。
在世雖有疑，當隨妙善法，
譬如觀岐道，利好者應逐。
復次，佛法之中，信為能入；若無信者，雖在佛法，終無所獲。如是等種種因緣覺知疑過，當急棄之。
en: Fifth, abandoning the hindrance of doubt: because doubt covers the mind, a concentrated mind cannot be attained with regard to any dharma whatsoever. And because a concentrated mind is absent, one gains nothing at all within the Buddhadharma — like a person entering a mountain of treasure who, having no hands, is unable to take anything at all. Furthermore, doubt in general is of very many kinds, and not all of it necessarily obstructs concentration. The doubt that truly obstructs concentration here refers to three specific kinds: doubt about oneself; doubt about one's teacher; and doubt about the Dharma.

Doubt about oneself: if a person thinks, "My faculties are dull and clouded, my offenses deep and grave — am I truly a fit vessel for this?" — giving rise to this self-doubt, the dharma of concentration will, in the end, never be brought forth. To remove this, one must not belittle oneself, since the depth of one's wholesome roots from past lives is difficult to measure.

Doubt about one's teacher: "That person's dignified bearing and outward appearance are of such a kind — they themselves lack the path, so how could they possibly teach me?" Giving rise to this kind of doubt and arrogance directly obstructs concentration. The method for removing it is as the Mahāyāna treatise says: "It is like gold within a foul-smelling leather sack — because one desires the gold, one does not discard the foul sack on that account. The practitioner should be exactly the same: even though a teacher may not be entirely pure, one should still give rise to the perception of them as a buddha." This matter is explained fully where the Mahāyāna treatise recounts Sadāprarudita's own seeking of a good spiritual friend — this should be explained in full there.

Doubt about the Dharma: people of the world mostly cling to their own original mind, unable to place immediate faith in the Dharma they have received, and so do not receive and practice it with a reverent mind. If the mind gives rise to hesitation and vacillation, the Dharma cannot color the spirit. Why is this? As the verse rejecting doubt says:
"Like a person standing at a forked road, doubtful and unsure, grasping at nothing —
So it is, exactly the same, with doubt regarding the true reality of all dharmas.
Because of doubt, one fails to diligently seek the true reality of all dharmas;
This doubt itself is born from delusion, and is the very worst among evils.
Amid wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, amid birth-and-death and nirvāṇa,
There is a fixed, real, and true dharma present — do not give rise to doubt regarding it.
If you harbor doubt and confusion, you are bound as though by the jailer of death and rebirth,
Like a deer seized in a lion's grip, unable to attain liberation.
While still in the world, though doubt may arise, one should follow the sublime and wholesome Dharma —
Just as, observing a forked road, one should follow whichever path is favorable and good."
Furthermore, within the Buddhadharma, faith alone is what allows one to enter; without faith, though one may remain within the Buddhadharma, nothing at all is ultimately gained. Through causes and conditions such as these, the fault of doubt is to be recognized, and it must be swiftly abandoned.

zh: 問曰：不善法塵無量，何故但棄五法？答曰：此五蓋中即有三毒等分為根本，亦得攝八萬四千塵勞門。所以者何？貪欲蓋即貪毒，瞋恚蓋即瞋毒，睡及疑此二蓋共為癡毒，當知即具三毒。掉悔蓋通從三毒起，即等分攝，合為四分煩惱。一中即有二萬一千，四中合有八萬四千，是故除此五蓋，即是除一切不善之法。行者如是等種種因緣棄於五蓋，譬如負債得脫，重病得差，如饑餓之人得至豐國，如於怨賊中得自免濟，安隱無患。行者亦如是，除此五蓋，其心安隱，清淨快樂。譬如日月以五事覆翳：煙、雲、塵、霧、羅睺阿修羅手障，則不能照。人亦如是。
en: Question: The unwholesome dharmas and defiling objects are measureless in number — why abandon only these five? Answer: Within these five hindrances are contained the three poisons together with the equal-portion affliction as their very root, and they are also able to encompass the eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction. Why is this? The hindrance of desire is precisely the poison of craving; the hindrance of anger is precisely the poison of aversion; the hindrances of sleep and doubt together constitute the poison of delusion — hence it can be known that the three poisons are already contained within them. The hindrance of restlessness and regret arises generally from all three poisons at once, and so belongs to the equal-portion affliction — together making four divisions of affliction in all. Within each one of these there are twenty-one thousand, and across all four together there are eighty-four thousand — hence removing these five hindrances is precisely removing every unwholesome dharma whatsoever.

The practitioner who abandons the five hindrances through causes and conditions such as these is like one freed from debt, or cured of a grave illness, or a starving person who has reached a land of plenty, or one who has escaped and been rescued from among enemies and thieves — at ease, in peace, and free of affliction. The practitioner is exactly the same: once these five hindrances are removed, the mind is at ease, pure, and joyful. It is like the sun and moon obscured by five things — smoke, cloud, dust, mist, and the hand of the asura Rāhu — unable to shine forth; a person is exactly the same.

This is the treatise's canonical account of the five hindrances (五蓋, nīvaraṇa) — sensory desire, ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt — a list so foundational to Buddhist meditation instruction generally that it recurs across nearly every tradition's practice manuals to this day. Two details are worth flagging: the fourfold mapping onto the three poisons plus "equal-portion" affliction (with the arithmetic 21,000 × 4 = 84,000 explaining the traditional count of "eighty-four thousand afflictions" found throughout Chinese Buddhist literature), and the specifically Buddhist analysis of "restlessness and regret" as two related but distinguishable problems rather than a single undifferentiated agitation. Restlessness belongs to the act itself; regret is of two kinds — the regret that arises afterward over that restlessness, and the lingering remorse of one who has committed a grave offense, which has nothing to do with restlessness at all. This closes 棄五蓋 (abandoning the five hindrances), the third of the twenty-five preliminary conditions' five groups.

quiz.q: How does the hindrance of desire differ from the earlier rejection of the five desires?
options: form realm versus desire realm
lay versus monastic
they are the same
the former concerns desire arising from the five external objects; this concerns desire arising from the internal faculty of mind
quiz.why: "What was described earlier concerns desire arising from the five external objects; here, desire arising from the internal faculty of intention is addressed. This refers to a practitioner sitting upright in the cultivation of dhyāna, giving rise to a mind of desire that continues moment after moment, covering over the wholesome mind."

quiz.q: How does the text arrive at the "nine grounds for vexation"?
options: three vexations in each realm
this person vexes me, vexes those dear to me, praises those I resent — and the same for past and future
three grades each of craving, aversion, delusion
one vexation per sequential concentration
quiz.why: "A practitioner, while sitting, may reflect: 'This person has vexed me, and has vexed those dear to me, and has praised those I resent.' Reflecting in the same way about the past and the future gives nine grounds for vexation in all."

quiz.q: When Śakra asked the Buddha in verse, how did the Buddha answer?
options: slay craving and there is peace
slay doubt and there is freedom from sorrow
slay sleep and there is peace
slay anger and there is peace and freedom from sorrow; anger is the root of poison and destroys every good
quiz.why: "Slay anger, and peace is attained; slay anger, and freedom from sorrow is attained. / Anger is the very root of poison; anger destroys every wholesome thing." Hence one cultivates loving-kindness and patience to remove it.

quiz.q: Why does the text say the hindrance of sleep is the most unwholesome and hard to remove?
options: because Māra produces it
other hindrances can be recognized and removed, but sleep is like a dead person with no awareness — unaware, it is hard to remove
because it belongs to the form realm
because the body needs sleep
quiz.why: "The remaining hindrances can still be recognized and removed by feeling and awareness, but sleep is like a dead person, possessing no awareness or consciousness whatsoever. Because there is no awareness of it, it is hard to remove and extinguish." When heavy, a meditation-weight or staff is used.

quiz.q: Restlessness is of three kinds. What is verbal restlessness?
options: chasing objects, occupied with literary arts
constant fear, the arrow of regret in the heart
wandering about and jesting, unable to sit still
a fondness for chanting, contending over right and wrong, idle and worldly talk
quiz.why: "Verbal restlessness is a fondness for chanting and reciting, contending over right and wrong, and idle conversation and worldly talk of no benefit." Wandering is bodily, chasing objects is mental, and the arrow of regret is the second kind of regret.

quiz.q: The doubt that truly obstructs concentration is of three kinds. Which?
options: doubt about Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha
doubt about cause, effect, condition
doubt about past, present, future
doubt about oneself, one's teacher, the Dharma
quiz.why: "The doubt that truly obstructs concentration here refers to three specific kinds: doubt about oneself; doubt about one's teacher; and doubt about the Dharma." Doubt in general is of many kinds and does not all obstruct concentration.

quiz.q: To remedy doubt about one's teacher, what simile does the text cite from the Mahāyāna treatise?
options: entering a treasure mountain without hands
a lion seizing a deer
gold in a foul leather sack — wanting the gold, one does not discard the sack; even if the teacher is impure, regard them as a buddha
standing at a fork in the road
quiz.why: "It is like gold within a foul-smelling leather sack — because one desires the gold, one does not discard the foul sack on that account. The practitioner should be exactly the same: even though a teacher may not be entirely pure, one should still give rise to the perception of them as a buddha." The treasure mountain and the forked road illustrate doubt in general and doubt about the Dharma.

quiz.q: Why abandon only five hindrances? How does the text map them onto the three poisons and the equal-portion affliction?
options: the hindrances are unrelated to the poisons
desire is delusion; sleep is craving
desire is craving; anger is aversion; sleep and doubt together are delusion; restlessness-regret arises from all three and is the equal portion; 21,000 each, 84,000 in all
doubt is aversion; restlessness is delusion
quiz.why: "The hindrance of desire is precisely the poison of craving; the hindrance of anger is precisely the poison of aversion; the hindrances of sleep and doubt together constitute the poison of delusion ... The hindrance of restlessness and regret arises generally from all three poisons at once, and so belongs to the equal-portion affliction ... Within each one of these there are twenty-one thousand, and across all four together there are eighty-four thousand."
